to turn back.
We waited at Canton for more favorable weather and now

night.

January 5 1936.

Dear Family:
It has been lo these many moons since you have been regaled or
bedeviled with any news letter concerning
the peregrinations of the
writer but now I am on the wing again and can write - this time
from Canton to Shanghai. My time has been spent largely between
Shanghai and Manila, mostly at the latter.
In fact I haven't been
back to Shanghai since leaving there on Sept. 10th, but have made three
rips from Manila to Macao across the turbulent China Sea which is
about as rough at times as the English Channel only it is 700 miles
The steamships which I have traveled on lately might just as
have closed down the cuisine department and redecorated
dining salon.
On one trip Dec. 9th and 10th I was the only passenger
apparently who saw anything but the ceiling of his or her stateroom.
When I went down to dinner there wasn't another customer out of a
passenger list of 40 so I dined in state complete with orchestra.
You would all like Macau.
It is an old Portuguese settlement
located about 40 miles west of Hongkong.
It was the Portuguese of
course who wére the first to discover a
trade route to China via the
Prior to the operation of the old Portuguese sailing ships all
of the silk, tea, spices, etc. of China moved to Europe by the Marco
Polo or other overland caravan routes
which were often interrupted
then as now by civil disturbances or wars along the way.
Portuguese traders settled at a point on the China Coast near Ningpo
south of Shanghai but such was the cruelty of their exploitation that
even the peaceful, defenseless Chinese finally couldn't "take it" any
longer with
result that they "swarmed" and massacred the entire
Portuguese Colony.
The Portuguese then looked around for some loc-
ation with a good harbor capable of being better defended.
selected 3 small peninsula south of the Pearl River important trade
route to Canton and settled there in 1557.
Macau soon became the
focal poifit for trade with China and Japan (before Japan closed its
doors to foreign traders).
The little Colony continued to thrive
and its residents prospered until the establishment of Hongkong.
The latter point was given to England by China in response to insis-
tant demands for the protection of English citizens.
Other nations
may adopt a conciliatory attitude and criticise their nationals for
straying off the reservation but the British have a way
of letting
everyone know that there is no open season on Englishmen.
The Chinese
at the time were highly gleeful over the way they had put it over on
the English - they had driven John Bull out of Canton and had given
him a barren rock off the forbidding coast to the north of the estuary of
the Pearl River.
The English of course soon transformed Hongkong into
one of the finest ports in
the world which with its unequalled facil-
ities for modern large draft ships soon began to get away all the
business from Canton and Macau neither of which could ofter proper
harbor facilities for the modern large ships which began to replace
the old sailing ships and the big sea-going junks.
Today Hongkong -
much to the chagrin of China - is the great port
There cargoes are trans-shipped to the seven seas.
still an important point for Chinese junks - thousands of them are
coming and going all the time with their picturesque sails of straw
matting or patched canvas.
All these junks plying in and around
Macau are heavily armed (against pirates or for operation as such)
with old fashioned cannons.
Most of the sea-going ones have two
guns
fore and two aft.
The cannons are of
the muzzle loading type
used during the War of 1812 with a hole at the back end for a fuse.

Page 2.
God knows what the Chinese load them with - probably for the most part
with the off-fall of Fords - bolts, screws,
washers,
bits of rusty iron,
I imagine if you got in the way of a
broadside and
survived with
a few scratches you would die of lockjaw within 24 hours.
Macao is sometimes referred to as
the wickedest city in the
There you can buy opium, or any kind of dope, a wife it you
need one from "white" slavers, or you can gamble at dens as numerous
along the main street as saloons used to be in Madison, Illinois.
gambling houses, have signs written in
Chinese, Portuguese and many
in English "First Class Gambling House."
The only foreign style Hotel is the Riviera which has about
twenty rooms - a few with bath but none with heat and when we first
got there (I went with C. S. Russell, P.A.A. Construction Engineer)
it was bitterly cold.
The kind of cold that you encounter only in
Florida or other tropical climates - a raw penetrating cold which you
can escape only by going to bea.
We bought an oil stove and rented
an electric heater and with both operating at wide open throttle we
managed to keep one room (our office) fairly comfortable using the
other room to sleep in.
Macau is the cleanest city I have ever seen - even the
Chinese districts are clean.
Every scrap of paper or cigarettes butt
is picked up or brushed away.
The streets are well paved with trees
lining both sides.
Houses are neat and clean built of brick or stone
with tile roofs.
They are mostly painted in shades of pastel pink,
blue, green or yellow.
It's as though a bit of old Europe had been
lifted up and put down on the China coast.
Most of the inhabitants are
Chinese - population of 85,000 with only 3000 Portuguese.
We were en-
tertained by the whole American community consisting of five. Mr. and
Mrs. Barrett, her sister (from Le Roy, N. Y.) and Mr. and Mrs. Servier.
The men are engineers in charge of the construction of a new water works
project for the Colony.
You have probably seen news reels and read about the first
arrival of the China Clipper at Manila.
Therefore I won't comment on
that event other than to say that it was thrilling and that after work-
ing for three years on some of the smaller factors involved in the
successful completion of the trans-Pacific flight I naturally got a
big kiok out of seeing that first plane land on the waters of Manila
Vle all had Christmas Eve together at Manila and then on
Christmas Day I had to start back to Macau leaving the family in Manila.
Stayed at Macao until New Years Eve which we (Russell and I) celebrated
by going to a movie "Broadway Melody", having a whiskey soda at the
Vittoria night club to welcome the New Year and then I winded my way
through the firecrackers smoke to the wharf where I took the night
boat for Hongkong to sleep on a cot without springs, a concrete pillow
and hope that the Indian guard on board would do their duty if any
pirates put in an appearance.
At Canton one of my Chinese friends gave me a snake dinner
prepared by the Number 1 snake chef of Canton.
The party of ten ate
20 snakes and as I ate more than my share it will be clear that I
"Boscoed" at least two.
You have undoubtedly heard that snakes
like chicken - that's true - but the snake wine was not so good.
wine tasted like corn liquor of a poor quality flavored with quinine.
However I managed to "gombey" (bottoms up to you) four or five small
cupsfull much to the gratification of my host and * intense discom-
forture of my almost rebellious tummy.
